Establish a fixed, clearly communicated timeline for processing and approval.

Avoid repeated submission of documents already available with the department, and enable reuse of previously submitted documents at renewal.

findings.text: Approval has taken anywhere from a week to nearly two years for different applicants; average is around 40 days but full clearance can take up to a year.
Application is filed online, but applicants must visit the department in person to learn what is pending or queried - the tracker does not reflect real status ('online in name only').
Existing license, architect-approved plan, challan and plot layout are all required together, with officials often asking for more details beyond the checklist.
Vacant officer posts (one approving officer had retired) slow down processing further.
Businesses often hire consultants (reported cost ~₹20,000) just to manage the paperwork for the application.
Some units are reportedly shifting or considering shifting operations to Tamil Nadu because of processing delays.
Long application form that is not easily understandable; applicants need more time to understand the terms and conditions.
The process requires the consent of several departments; applicants may need to follow up with various departments.
3 copies of documents are submitted to the department, which provides 1 copy back to the applicant, creating extra printing and paperwork.
Fees are levied based on plot/land area, and applicants are unsure about the exact cost since it keeps changing.
Need for a more integrated single-window approval mechanism and a reduction in the number of departments from which approvals are required.
Approval procedures should be standardised across departments, with requirements clearly defined and communicated.
Application fee was described as nominal by participants in one session.
Provisional approval lets a unit start work early, though final validity depends on the project and any later change to the factory.
Move query resolution and follow-up online so applicants don't need to visit in person; keep the status tracker updated in real time.
Fill vacant officer posts to clear the backlog.

findings.text: Fire NOC's one-year validity is shorter than Pollution Control and Factories approvals (5 years) and the Education department's approval (3 years).
The same full set of documents is resubmitted every year at renewal, even when nothing at the premises has changed.

High compliance cost: fire exits, sprinklers and extinguishers can cost ₹2-3 lakh the first time, with yearly refilling alone costing close to ₹50,000; for higher-risk units the cost can run up to ₹50 lakh.
A separate, uncapped third-party inspection fee is paid: reported as ~₹25,000 for small establishments and up to ₹5 lakh for large establishments (e.g. 40-acre sites).
Applicants are often unsure whether the fire department itself or a private third-party agency is inspecting the premises.
A file is sometimes sent back or rejected after inspection without the department stating exactly what needs to be fixed.
Deemed approval exists for departmental delays, but most applicants are not aware of it and officials are reluctant to use it when fire-safety arrangements are not yet in place.
No real status tracking beyond broad labels (initiated, resubmitted, completed); no visibility into which officer is holding the file.
Process remains manual/visit-based - hard copies submitted in person and queries communicated informally, often by phone, despite the online form.
Turnaround time and queries raised vary depending on which Fire Officer or zone the unit falls under.
Industrial units undergo a two-step inspection - first by a departmental official and again by a third-party agency - before the file reaches the Fire Officer for final approval.
Inspection timing depends on the third-party agency's own availability, adding to the wait.
Mandatory physical inspections increase overall processing time; non-compliance found during inspection requires corrective action before approval.
Application requirements and compliance guidelines are not sufficiently clear for first-time applicants; the portal does not reflect additional consultancy/intermediary costs.

A uniform compliance checklist is followed despite different fire-safety needs across sectors; high-risk industries (plastic, packaging, pharmaceutical) face comparatively higher compliance requirements.
One session (FNO_1) reports Fire NOC renewal is required every 6 months, conflicting with the other two sessions' and the ED's one-year validity figure.
Extend Fire NOC validity to at least three years, in line with the renewal cycle other departments already follow.
Add a real status tracker showing the actual stage of a file and which officer is holding it.
Give written reasons for queries and clarify up front which part of inspection is departmental vs third-party, along with the applicable fee.
No statutory fee is charged directly on the portal for submitting the Fire NOC application; most applicants are self-filed without a consultant for the basic process.

findings.text: Suitable industrial plots are not readily available when applicants require them; some vacant plots may not be available for immediate allotment.

Pending allotment can delay construction, machinery investment and other project activities; subsequent approvals such as electricity connection may depend on allotment documents.
Applicants have to undergo physical inspection/verification as part of the land allotment process.
The process involves application scrutiny, inspection, evaluation and final allotment - multiple stages that can increase the time taken to receive a decision.
Applicants may have to provide project-related information already submitted online again, and may need to carry physical copies of documents despite online submission.
Some industrial plots remain vacant for long periods, while new applicants continue to seek land.

Create a real-time land availability dashboard clearly displaying available, allotted, vacant and under-process plots.
Provide time-bound application processing with defined timelines for scrutiny, inspection, evaluation and final allotment, with status updates at each stage.
Regularly review long-vacant plots and make eligible plots available for fresh allotment to prospective applicants.
Uncertainty regarding land allotment can make applicants hesitant to commit funds towards construction, machinery and other project-related investments.

findings.text: The payment gateway sometimes experiences technical issues, particularly during renewal payments.
The licence is renewed annually, requiring applicants to undertake the renewal application process every year, which requires conscious effort even though the process is online.

Verification is also carried out during the renewal process; no separate inspection fee is paid as the applicable renewal fee covers it.
The same documents must be submitted again during each renewal application even when there is no change in information.
The overall licence process is generally reported to take approximately one to two months, though individual experiences varied with inspection timelines.
Participants did not report a significant business or financial impact from approval delays, since applicants generally apply well in advance.
There was minimal to no reliance on intermediaries; users are comfortable applying directly for the licence.
The major cost concern raised was not the statutory application fee but the Trade Licence cost, reported to be significantly higher.
Extend the licence renewal period to five years instead of requiring annual renewal, as followed in some other states.
Enable applicants to reuse documents already uploaded in previous applications, with modifications permitted only where required.
Review the requirement for the Trade Licence as a prerequisite for Legal Metrology, given its comparatively higher cost.

findings.text: Renewal reported to take anywhere from ~3-4 months (one session, with some cases longer) to 'well over a year', more than one and a half years for some categories (another session).
Other departments such as Inspector of Factories, Panchayat and Fire informally keep their own licenses pending until the pollution consent renewal comes through.
Deemed approval is known to exist on paper but is not followed/enforced by the department in practice.
The same condition-point compliance details, monitoring reports and company documents must be re-uploaded in full at every renewal.
Applications are sometimes rejected close to the end of the processing window on technical grounds, forcing the applicant to start over with a fresh application.
Pollution-control equipment upgrades (e.g. retrofitting a small backup generator) can cost nearly as much as replacement, disproportionate for rarely-used equipment.
The application gets a unique login ID and portal tracking, but the file still needs to be picked up by an assigned officer, and progress depends on reaching that person directly.
No fixed/standard instruction exists on which drawings to upload; the requirement varies by inspector.
Simple detail changes such as a registered email ID cannot be done online, requiring a fresh demand draft and manual follow-up.

gaps.text: The two FGD sessions report substantially different renewal timelines - one describes ~3-4 months (with some cases longer), the other describes 'well over a year' and more than 1.5 years for some categories; both exceed anything the ED's stated process (~7-day scrutiny + 7-day rectification window) would suggest, and the ED itself states the actual overall timeline 'is not specifically stated'.

FGD participants describe a deemed-approval provision 'known to applicants' that exists 'on paper' but isn't enforced, while the ED states no deemed-approval provision is specified for CTO renewal at all under the current OCMMS process - a difference in whether a renewal-specific deemed-approval rule is understood by applicants to exist.

ED does not address the copy-count difference (3 vs 7 hard copies depending on location inside/outside an industrial estate), or the inability to make minor online corrections (e.g. email ID) without a fresh demand draft - both added by FGD.
ED does not mention departmental delay being billed back to applicants as a penalty/regularisation charge; this is a notable FGD-only pain point.

Neither source quantifies how the category classification (by employee count) maps to specific fee slabs for renewal.

findings.text: The portal is slow during application submission, causing delays for users.
No dedicated helpdesk is available for users facing issues or queries during the application process.
If the application is not processed within the expected time, users do not get deemed approval and have to wait for the department's approval.
The renewal process is time-consuming, requiring users to spend additional time completing the process after certificate validity ends.
No expiry reminder is given before registration lapses, and the process is not integrated with other departmental portals, requiring information/documents to be provided again.
Employee-related details must be entered individually instead of being able to upload the complete list at once.
Users may have to submit documents again during renewal even when there is no change, and details already provided earlier may need to be entered again.
The process is largely online, with no physical inspection in normal cases and no physical document submission.
The concerned department is reported to be approachable when users need clarification or assistance.
Users did not consider the basic documentation requirement to be a major difficulty in the process.
Improve portal speed and performance, and provide a dedicated helpdesk or online support facility.
Introduce deemed approval where the application is not processed within the prescribed time.
Simplify the renewal process by allowing existing registration details to be carried forward, and introduce expiry reminders (SMS/email).
Enable document and data integration so that information already available with the government does not have to be submitted again.

FGD does not confirm or dispute the ED's uncertain 7-vs-9-day timeline figure; FGD instead frames the issue purely as 'no deemed approval,' without citing a specific number of days.

gaps.text: FGD participants report an informal payment/bribe being sought 'during the physical inspection process' for Trade License Approval, while the ED explicitly states that 'physical inspection before approval has been removed under a new by-law' for this service - raising a question of whether this refers to a different/earlier inspection stage (e.g. occupancy-certificate verification) not reconciled in either transcript.

This FGD session was comparatively thin (6 participants, short discussion), reporting 'no policy issues,' 'no procedural issues,' and 'no reason for delay' - it does not corroborate or contradict most of the ED's detailed findings (e.g. the 2-3 month NOC delays, the 27-vs-3-4 document count) one way or the other.

findings.text: The source file's 'Pain Points' table content describes industrial land-allotment/plot-availability issues, not Trade License Renewal; this appears to be a copy-paste error in the underlying transcript file - findings below draw only on the sections and quotes clearly tagged 'Trade License - Renewal'.
No clearly communicated timeline for when the renewed licence will be approved; processing time can vary by category of business.
Certain applicants are asked to obtain approvals/NOCs from other departments, increasing compliance burden.
Even after applying online, users still have to submit documents physically.
Repeated physical follow-up is needed with the department after submitting the application.
Verification and document scrutiny take considerable time before the application moves toward approval.
No application tracking is available - users cannot see whether the application is under scrutiny, pending a query, or ready for approval.
A query-resubmission-follow-up cycle exists: queries can require another submission and subsequent follow-up before approval.
Notes mention consultancy cost and, in some cases, informal payment/favour concerns linked to involvement of other departments.
No specific redundant/duplicate document pain point was confirmed in the notes for this session.
Make the process completely end-to-end online, removing physical submission wherever not essential, and introduce application tracking.
Display a clear approval timeline for each business category and show NOC requirements upfront, before the application is submitted.
Enable online query resolution so users can respond to queries and upload documents through the portal, reducing physical follow-up.

gaps.text: The ED describes Trade Licence Renewal as 'auto-approved instantly on payment of the renewal fee, with the licence available for download the same day', with no document scrutiny and no in-person visit required. FGD participants instead report that 'even after applying online, we still have to submit the documents physically', that 'inspection and document checking takes a lot of time', and that repeated follow-up is needed - a substantial contradiction on whether renewal is instant/auto-approved or document-scrutinised and visit-based.

The source FGD document's own 'Pain Points' table (and part of its 'Policy Issues' table) appear to describe industrial land-allotment issues (plot availability, Allotment Committee) rather than Trade Licence Renewal - likely a drafting/copy-paste error in the underlying transcript file; this extraction relies on the sections and the quotes table that are unambiguously tagged 'Trade License - Renewal'.
Neither source quantifies how much longer the 'category-based variation in processing time' actually runs for different business categories.
